prize_parts.citation: for the development of nanopores for electrical reading of single DNA and RNA molecules

statement.case_for: Nanopore sensing rests on one transparent principle: a single polynucleotide threaded through a molecular-scale channel modulates the ionic current, and the current reports chemical identity. Deamer supplied the conceptual origin, Akeson showed that an enzyme can ratchet the strand through the pore slowly enough to read it, and Bayley engineered the protein pores and the chemistry that made the readout robust. The result is a quantitative, label-free, long-read analytical capability that is in wide field use, independently reproduced, and now extends to modified bases, RNA and peptides. It is mature, it opened applications nobody foresaw, and it can be explained to a broad audience in one sentence.
statement.case_against: The idea has several fathers. Kasianowicz, Branton, Deamer and Brandin demonstrated translocation in 1996, so a three-person cut that leaves out Branton and Kasianowicz needs a defensible rule, and I am uneasy that the prize would partly reward a commercial sequencing technology that is as much engineering and instrumentation as chemistry. Several colleagues also fairly ask whether the central advance belongs to chemistry or to physics and genomics. The candidate has only two first-place or top-three votes, so its breadth of support is thin compared with B056.

responses.point: Chabes ranks PROTACs and molecular glues first: induced proximity makes a small molecule a catalytic tool for removing any protein, and the cereblon discovery explained thalidomide.
responses.response: I agree this is the broadest-based candidate on the table; eight of us ranked it, and I placed it sixth only because I look for a quantitative physical principle and for maturity. The mechanism is real, but no PROTAC drug is approved and the Crews, Deshaies, Handa trio leaves out Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Kim and Ito, with the PROTAC line and the glue line arguably two different discoveries. I would accept it as the fallback if the committee prefers a field with the widest support, but I ask that we settle first whether it is one prize part or two before we draft a citation.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics first: a clean 1985 origin, two names, four decades of use, and recognition that is overdue.
responses.response: I share this view and ranked it third; it is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I have no scientific reservation. My difference is one of order: a methods prize in simulation has fewer people who can judge it from outside theoretical chemistry, whereas nanopores give a concrete new analytical capability. Johan, what is the best argument that the sequencing impact of nanopores is more engineering than chemistry, so that I can test my own ranking against it?

responses.point: Zou ranks halide perovskites first as a designed crystal architecture with a new function, efficiencies rivaling silicon, and a large structure-property literature.
responses.response: I ranked perovskites second for generative potential and for the physics of defect tolerance, but I would qualify the maturity point. Stability, lead content and scale-up are unresolved, and the attribution is the most crowded on the list: Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis each have a serious claim, and the three-person cut would be contested. Compared with nanopores, the discovery question of who did what and when is harder to answer cleanly here.

responses.point: Aili ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first as molecular design that made siRNA and mRNA medicines deliverable, and ranks nanopores third while doubting whether Branton is still alive.
responses.response: I take the lipid nanoparticle case seriously on impact, and the complementarity with the 2023 Medicine prize is a fair point. My reservation is attribution: six credited names across Vancouver, MIT and elsewhere, and a real question whether the decisive step is lipid design or formulation, so a three-person set will be hard to defend. On Branton, I cannot confirm his status from the files I am allowed to read, so my configuration avoids relying on him and I treat his and Kasianowicz's omission as a general attribution issue we must justify.

responses.point: Sparr ranks lipid nanoparticles first and phase separation second, both as soft-matter physics applied to biology, and calls the condensate concept broadly adopted but still contested in vivo.
responses.response: I share your interest in the physical-chemical framing and ranked condensates fourth for that reason, but I agree with your own caution that the field is young and contested on which in-cell assemblies are truly phase-separated. That is the reason I would not put it ahead of a method that is mature and independently confirmed. I would like your view on whether the lipid nanoparticle trio you propose, Cullis, Madden and Hope, is defensible without Anderson and Langer, since that cut decides whether the candidate is viable.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-person nanopore trio that omits Branton and Kasianowicz, and whether Branton's status affects eligibility.
Whether nanopore sequencing is judged to be chemistry or primarily instrumentation and genomics.
Whether PROTACs and molecular glues should be treated as one prize part or two, and whether the absence of an approved degrader makes recognition premature.
How strongly the 2024 protein prize and the 2023 Medicine mRNA prize should weigh for or against the candidates close to them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates; I am a nanophysicist at Lund University working on nanowire devices and molecular motors, with no stated connection to the nanopore, perovskite, degrader or lipid nanoparticle investigators. I note that two committee colleagues, Somfai and Sparr, are also at Lund, which is not a conflict for any candidate.
